/uk-news/2026/nov/18/doctor-whose-eviden.headline: Thirlwall inquiry has left biggest questions around the Letby case unanswered
/uk-news/2026/nov/18/doctor-whose-eviden.excerpt: Just two months before Lady Justice Kathryn Thirlwall opened her inquiry into events at the Countess of Chester hospital and the crimes of Lucy Letby, a report by Chris Henley KC was published into the “atrocious” wrongful conviction of Andrew Malkinson for rape. Henley prefaced that report with a plea for the legal establishment to recognise that the criminal courts produce miscarriages of justice. Right up to top judges in the court of appeal, Henley wrote, the system has “a deep-seated … cultural reluctance” to accept it “will on occasion make mistakes” and that “entirely innocent defendants will sometimes be convicted”. He said the system needed a culture that acknowledges mistakes can be made and ensures “in our various roles when making decisions we are all alive to this potential risk”. The Thirlwall inquiry was set up in 2023 by the then health secretary, Steve Barclay, on the basis that Letby was guilty of murdering seven babies, and attempting to murder seven more, at the Countess of Chester hospital’s neonatal unit where she was a nurse. Thirlwall’s terms of reference were to spotlight the hospital’s management, and whether their actions and culture “contributed to the failure to protect babies from Lucy Letby”. Many distinguished experts had already looked at the evidence and expressed very serious concerns that the system had made another of its mistakes and convicted an entirely innocent person.
/uk-news/2026/nov/18/doctor-whose-eviden.trail: Decision not to pause proceedings means £18m report does not engage with concerns over former nurse’s conviction

/politics/2026/nov/18/eu-uk-reset-summit.headline: Cheese, pet passports and youth mobility: what’s in the UK-EU ‘relationship reset’ draft?
/politics/2026/nov/18/eu-uk-reset-summit.excerpt: The UK-EU “relationship reset” agreement, which began in earnest under Keir Starmer, is expected to be signed off by Andy Burnham in Brussels on Friday. A leaked text of the second draft shows an agreement has largely been reached with some outstanding points. Here’s what is and isn’t addressed in the 72-paragraph joint communique, from pet passports and cheese imports to student fees and artist touring visas. I’m 29 – will the under-30s youth mobility scheme help me live in an EU country? You may not make it. The deal states it will “allow people from the EU and the UK to reside for up to three years to engage in activities such as work, studies, au pairing, volunteering, or simply travelling”. But the deal may not be active until 2030 because work permits are the preserve of national governments, not something Brussels can solve. “We aim to apply this agreement no later than 2028 and endeavour to ensure that opportunities under the scheme will be available to our young people no later than January 2030,” the draft says. I am an EU student. I want to apply for a year’s study in the UK. Will I pay home fees? This has yet to be agreed. The two options in the draft text are a halfway house between international and home fees, or a concession from the UK to allow EU citizens pay the same as British students (or Irish ones, who are also eligible for home fees under a separate longstanding agreement).
/politics/2026/nov/18/eu-uk-reset-summit.trail: Leaked text of 72-paragraph second draft shows agreement has largely been reached before expected signoff on Friday

/politics/2026/nov/18/eu-uk-reset-summit.headline: Burnham should fight next election on promise to rejoin EU, says Peter Kyle
/politics/2026/nov/18/eu-uk-reset-summit.excerpt: Andy Burnham should fight the next election on a promise to rejoin the EU, the former business secretary Peter Kyle has said, with voters given a referendum on the outcome of any deal. The Labour MP, a key member of Keir Starmer’s cabinet, said the “only way through” the challenges of the domestic political debate was for the government to offer voters the choice to accept or reject any agreement. His intervention comes as the prime minister prepares for a major UK-EU summit in Brussels on Friday, at which he hopes to secure agreements on food and farming and emissions trading. Burnham has said there was “no rush” to decide on the UK’s longer-term relationship with the EU, as he came under pressure from his own party to slow the pace of the promised pursuit of closer ties. Despite his suggestions at Labour conference, he is now not expected to set out the full options for a closer EU relationship until his 10-year plan in December – although he has denied he is “stepping back” from commitments. Kyle is the latest senior Labour figure to publicly wade into the Brexit debate after the former foreign secretary David Lammy said the party should go into the next election clear that its intention was to rejoin. Rachel Reeves, the former chancellor, has also argued Britain’s future should be back in the bloc, arguing that leaving had made the UK “poorer, weaker and less secure”.
/politics/2026/nov/18/eu-uk-reset-summit.trail: Exclusive: Former business secretary calls for Labour manifesto commitment with referendum on final decision

/politics/2026/nov/18/eu-uk-reset-summit.headline: Brexit work travel rules need urgent improvement, say UK business leaders
/politics/2026/nov/18/eu-uk-reset-summit.excerpt: Business chiefs have called on the UK government and the European Commission to urgently ease Brexit restrictions on business travel for cross-Channel work trips. A group representing industry bosses said it wants commitments from Andy Burnham and European political leaders that the restrictions will be one of the priorities in 2027 for furthering ties between the two sides, after a summit in Brussels this week. The Confederation of British Industry (CBI), which represents some of Britain’s largest companies, welcomed the prime minister’s recent calls for a reset with Europe, designed to reverse some of the damage to Britain’s economy caused by Brexit. But it said Brexit restrictions, which include making employees obtain work permits for travel, are deterring cross-border investors and hampering trade at the very time both sides are trying to build resilience against China. Sean McGuire, the CBI’s director of Europe and international, said discussions should have been a priority in the talks this week, after a UK-EU summit in 2025 held by Keir Starmer also referenced improving business mobility. “Very little has been achieved. In fact, practically nothing has been achieved. The emphasis was put on youth mobility,” said McGuire. EU diplomats have said in the past that the UK pushed hard for improving business mobility but was met with resistance from the bloc, where member states see British services – a big export particularly in the financial sector – as a threat.
/politics/2026/nov/18/eu-uk-reset-summit.trail: CBI says cross-Channel business trips urgently need to be made easier to support investment and trade

/politics/2026/nov/18/eu-uk-reset-summit.headline: Is £750m a week the real cost of rejoining the EU – or the Brexit bus myth all over again?
/politics/2026/nov/18/eu-uk-reset-summit.excerpt: A new analysis from some of the architects of the Vote Leave campaign has claimed rejoining the EU would cost Britain £750m a week. How did they arrive at these figures – and are they any more reliable than the ones on the side of the bus? What is behind Stay Out’s claim that rejoining the EU would cost '£750m a week'? Stay Out calculates that it would cost £750m a week to rejoin the EU (rounded down from £756m). The campaign group has based its analysis on the European Commission’s proposed long-term EU budget, worth €2tn (£1.66tn) over 2028-34. The group assumes that Britain rejoining the EU would increase the budget and the UK would make a contribution commensurate with its size and wealth. The £750m is a gross figure, excluding funds that would return to Britain, such as farm subsidy payments and scientific grants. It follows the method of Vote Leave, which was reprimanded by the UK Statistics Authority in 2016 for its “misleading” claim that Britain’s EU membership cost £350m a week. That statistic, emblazoned on the side of a campaign bus, did not count the British rebate or EU funds that flowed to the UK. Stay Out’s headline statistic could be seen as repeating the same trick. While its workings document states the £750m is a gross figure, that is not made clear in a campaign video likely to have far greater reach. “£750m a week: that is what the EU will charge us to rejoin” claims the video, replete with portentous music and images of streets on fire.
/politics/2026/nov/18/eu-uk-reset-summit.trail: A new analysis from some of the architects of the Vote Leave campaign is very selective with its figures

/politics/2026/nov/18/eu-uk-reset-summit.headline: Burnham says Brexit has dramatically diminished Britain’s global standing
/politics/2026/nov/18/eu-uk-reset-summit.excerpt: Britain’s global standing has diminished in the decade since Brexit, Andy Burnham has said, as he again signalled that Labour could drop its red lines on Europe in its next manifesto. In a foreign policy speech, Burnham said that after a major Brussels summit this week he would begin new discussions with the EU about options for “our long-term relationship”. However, the prime minister warned the process would take time and – amid concerns among some cabinet ministers that reopening Brexit divides could be a mistake – insisted that “at every stage the British people will be the boss”. Burnham is expected to begin setting out the broad options for forging a closer relationship, including a customs union, the single market and fully rejoining. He will stress that Labour will do nothing to cross its red lines this side of the next general election, with some inside government suggesting he should “press the brakes” a little on reversing Brexit rather than rushing ahead. Downing Street sources said Burnham wanted to “frame the debate” rather than pushing automatically to an end point. However, they admitted he had potentially made that more difficult by setting out his personal preference to rejoin the bloc.
/politics/2026/nov/18/eu-uk-reset-summit.trail: Prime minister signals Labour could drop its Brexit red lines in major foreign policy speech

/world/2026/nov/19/kerch-bridge-crimea-r.headline: Ukraine war briefing: US criticism of Kyiv’s deep strikes in Russia is ‘quite stupid’, says Germany
/world/2026/nov/19/kerch-bridge-crimea-r.excerpt: The Pentagon has warned Ukraine’s western backers that strikes deep inside Russia are counterproductive and urged them to focus their military support on equipment for frontline combat. Germany immediately dismissed the warning as “stupid,” while Britain said the strikes are saving lives. The disagreement came as Ukraine’s supporters met at Nato headquarters on Tuesday to rally support for more arms and ammunition. Speaking in Brussels, Pentagon policy ⁠chief Elbridge Colby said that “while the public conversation focuses on the spectacle of deep strikes designed to incur pain on the Russian population, our assessment is that such strikes have not been effective in driving an end to the war, nor do they contribute to blunting Russia’s advances on the front line.” He warned that deep strikes, “especially those that target civilian infrastructure such as Wildberries (the Russian equivalent of Amazon), have ‌actually probably hardened the Russian public’s resolve and the Kremlin’s own willingness to escalate”. He said his comments did not mean “Ukraine should be forced to fight with its hands tied behind its back”. Colby added that Ukraine’s army is “very effective” when it focuses on frontline fighting, using drones to slow Russian advances and hit their supply lines.
/world/2026/nov/19/kerch-bridge-crimea-r.trail: Pentagon policy ⁠chief’s comments on Ukraine’s war tactic sparks disagreement at Nato meeting. What we know on day 1,729

/world/2026/nov/19/kerch-bridge-crimea-r.headline: ‘They were keeping it for a rainy day’: Ukraine’s Kerch bridge attack is proof Kyiv still has cards to play
/world/2026/nov/19/kerch-bridge-crimea-r.excerpt: Ukraine’s attack on the Kerch road bridge overnight is the culmination of weeks, and perhaps months, of military operations plus years of industrial development, during which Kyiv has developed its own cruise missiles and long-range drones. The demolition is not quite total, because the rail bridge is still standing, one line in operation – but the attack is an obvious embarrassment to Russia two days before Vladimir Putin is due to meet Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in Shenzhen. Such is the collapse of a span of the roadway, and the loss of its supporting arch above, it appears to be a level of damage that “cannot be repaired any time soon”, says Ben Hodges, a former commanding general of the US army in Europe. The 19km (12-mile), $3.6bn (£2.7bn) road bridge connecting Russia to the east of Crimea was completed in 2018, a project closely associated with Putin and his efforts to secure the 2014 annexation of Crimea by opening up a supply route to the peninsula. Russia’s leader was filmed driving an orange truck into Crimea, greeted by cheering workers once the construction was complete. “Putin initiated this project himself,” the Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, said at the time. That was four years before Putin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which has, if anything, made Russia’s position in Crimea more precarious, though the change in the balance of power is a while coming.
/world/2026/nov/19/kerch-bridge-crimea-r.trail: Partial demolition of bridge linking Russia and occupied Crimea is obvious embarrassment to Putin days before meeting with Xi and Trump

/world/2026/nov/19/kerch-bridge-crimea-r.headline: Ukraine hits Kerch bridge between Russia and occupied Crimea
/world/2026/nov/19/kerch-bridge-crimea-r.excerpt: Ukraine has hit the Kerch bridge connecting occupied Crimea with Russia, in a symbolic blow that temporarily paralysed road traffic and left thousands of drivers stranded. A Ukrainian kamikaze drone crashed into one of the bridge’s arches at 5.38am local time, local channels reported. Earlier drones could be heard buzzing above the structure, as Russian air defence units opened fire. The extent of the damage was unclear. One report said the arch was listing at a 15-degree angle and “looked tired”. The Kremlin-appointed governor of Crimea, Sergey Aksyonov, confirmed the “enemy” had launched an attack. “As a result, traffic will be restricted, likely until the afternoon,” he wrote on Telegram. Russian officials said the crossing would remain closed while experts assessed its condition. About 2,000 vehicles were reportedly stuck in traffic jams on both sides. In a call with reporters, the Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, downplayed the incident. He said: “Minor damage is being assessed. ⁠Traffic across the bridge continues.” Ukraine says the bridge is a legitimate target for its armed forces, and has made at least two previous attempts to blow it up. In 2022 a truck laden with explosives damaged part of the road section. A second strike using a “sea baby” drone took place the following year. Russia has subsequently strengthened air defences and installed metal barges and boom barriers.
/world/2026/nov/19/kerch-bridge-crimea-r.trail: Traffic temporarily restricted on key connection after bridge targeted during overnight drone barrage by Ukraine

/world/2026/nov/19/mike-lynch-superyacht.headline: Pork fat, a heating pad and a five-storey jump: how a 74-year-old escaped house arrest in Argentina
/world/2026/nov/19/mike-lynch-superyacht.excerpt: As dozens of police and sniffer dogs poured into San Telmo, a traditional Buenos Aires neighbourhood with cobblestone streets, on Tuesday morning, one of the clerks at a shop selling dulce de leche asked them why. He said they were “looking for a bomb”. It was only later that she found out there was no danger of being blown up after all, and that authorities were, in fact, hunting for a fugitive. “An Italian mafioso, right?” she asked. The escapee was no mobster, exactly: he was Leonardo Bertulazzi, 74, a former member of Italy’s radical far-left militant group the Red Brigades, who had been living under house arrest in Argentina after his arrest in 2024, awaiting extradition to Italy to serve a 27-year sentence. On Tuesday, however, the 74-year-old escaped from house arrest in dramatic fashion. “It was like something out of a movie,” said a person with knowledge of the investigation who asked to remain anonymous. At around 6am, when most security forces “were focused on the Pope’s security” as the pontiff was visiting Argentina, Bertulazzi cut off his ankle monitor, the source said. In order to bypass its temperature and pressure sensors, Bertulazzi apparently wrapped it in a tube with pork fat and left it next to a heating pad. He then rappelled down from his apartment’s fifth floor, jumped in to a vacant lot behind the building, and then scaled a metal gate to reach the street.
/world/2026/nov/19/mike-lynch-superyacht.trail: Leonardo Bertulazzi, ex-member of Italy’s radical far-left Red Brigades, fled in dramatic fashion, ‘like something out of a movie’

/world/2026/nov/19/mike-lynch-superyacht.headline: ‘Like priests who don’t believe in God’: Italy’s anti-vax medics eye return to frontline duty
/world/2026/nov/19/mike-lynch-superyacht.excerpt: Antonio Cremasco contracted Covid at a dinner party on 6 March 2020. Four days later, as Italy became the first European country to go into nationwide lockdown, he was fighting for his life. “I spent 20 days in intensive care, followed by another 20 days in a hospital ward,” said Cremasco, from Bassano del Grappa in the northern Italian Veneto region. After leaving hospital, he needed oxygen therapy for another six months. Cremasco’s ordeal was such that when Covid vaccines became available in Italy in early 2021, he had no qualms about being vaccinated, and he believes the decision saved his life once again. “All those who had been in intensive care with me died,” he said. “Without the vaccine, if I had caught Covid again, I had a high risk of dying too.” But Cremasco, who is now 76 and recently received his annual Covid and winter flu jab, has struggled to convince his vaccine-sceptic son, a father of two, of the drugs’ safety. He said he and his wife were wary of having their potentially unvaccinated grandchildren in their home whenever the children were ill, fearing for their own health. “They always seem to be sick,” Cremasco said. His family rift mirrors a wider divide over vaccination in Italy, which has been brought back to the political spotlight by a controversial bill approved in October in the lower house of parliament.
/world/2026/nov/19/mike-lynch-superyacht.trail: Progress of bill to reinstate struck-off doctors hinged on support from far right figure Roberto Vannacci, whose rise is shaping politics before 2027 elections

/world/2026/nov/19/mike-lynch-superyacht.headline: Ex-member of radical Marxist group scales balcony, escapes house arrest in Argentina
/world/2026/nov/19/mike-lynch-superyacht.excerpt: A 74-year-old former member of Italy’s radical Marxist group the Red Brigades has escaped from house arrest in Argentina, the country’s security ministry confirmed on Wednesday, after he reportedly hid his ankle monitor inside a tube of pork and lowered himself from a fifth-floor balcony. Authorities placed Leonardo Bertulazzi under house arrest in Buenos Aires in 2024, prior to his extradition to Italy to serve a 27-year prison sentence. He had received the sentence in 1987 for joining a subversive association and belonging to an armed group. After years on the run, Bertulazzi was first arrested by Argentine authorities in 2002. He was freed a few months later and secured refugee status in 2004, but was arrested again in 2024 after it was revoked. On Wednesday, Argentina’s security ministry offered a $13,000 reward for information leading to Bertulazzi’s recapture after he slipped out of detention. The fugitive held a senior position in the Red Brigades, a radical Marxist organization responsible for attacks from 1969 to 1980, dubbed Italy’s “Years of Lead”. The group most notoriously kidnapped and assassinated former prime minister Aldo Moro in 1978. Security footage showed Bertulazzi dropping from a building into a public road as cars drove past. A detective tracking the former member of the Red Brigades reportedly told La Nación that Bertulazzi rappelled down from the fifth floor using a harness.
/world/2026/nov/19/mike-lynch-superyacht.trail: Leonardo Bertulazzi, 74, awaiting extradition to Italy, reportedly used harness to flee custody

/world/2026/nov/19/mike-lynch-superyacht.headline: KFC’s arrival at Italian ski slopes angers food and mountain purists
/world/2026/nov/19/mike-lynch-superyacht.excerpt: Skiers on the slopes of two of Italy’s most prestigious resorts will be able to dine from buckets of fried chicken between runs this winter as the US fast-food chain KFC prepares to open outlets, infuriating mountain and food purists while prompting a prominent businessman to threaten legal action. KFC will open its first high-altitude restaurants on the slopes of Cortina d’Ampezzo and Madonna di Campiglio, in the Dolomites, on 5 December, an initiative the company said was aimed at “surprising people” and “reaching places” where nobody would expect to find it. The move marks a debut for any fast-food outlet on an Italian ski slope, bringing a menu replete with KFC’s most popular products, from spicy wings and burgers to traditional buckets of fried chicken. The plans appear to have taken people by surprise, not least Alberico Zardini, a majority shareholder in Faloria Spa, the company that manages the infrastructure on Mount Faloria in Cortina d’Ampezzo, where there is to be a KFC at 2,123 metres. “The mere idea is disgraceful,” Zardini told Il Messaggero. “It’s absurd and shameful to imagine a fast-food joint in the most beautiful spot in Cortina. Do the people of Cortina not realise what we’re risking here?” Zardini said he had written to the bosses of Faloria warning that he would pursue legal action unless they put the brakes on KFC’s mountain ambitions.
/world/2026/nov/19/mike-lynch-superyacht.trail: Fast-food outlets at two prestigious Dolomites resorts are Italy’s first, with legal action threatened

/world/2026/nov/19/mike-lynch-superyacht.headline: ‘A global political awakening’: how gen Z protests are sweeping the world
/world/2026/nov/19/mike-lynch-superyacht.excerpt: In Brazil, they rallied online by the millions, sharing videos and spreading memes. In Serbia, they cycled across Europe and ran ultramarathons to make their voices heard. Both movements burst into international public view last month as they became central during election campaigns to the pushback against authoritarianism. What they also offered, however, was a window into a wider phenomenon playing out across the globe, as youth-led movements reshape political landscapes. “Gen Z is rising,” said Erica Chenoweth, a political scientist at Harvard Kennedy School. “It is abundantly clear that a significant proportion of gen Z is tired of sitting on the sidelines while their political systems fail them.” Researchers have documented at least 25 protests around the world in which this age group – roughly those between the ages of 14 and 29 – has played a role. From Bangladesh to Belgium and Italy to India, it seems gen Z, who account for about a third of the world’s population, have found their voice. “Gen Z may be experiencing a global political awakening,” Chenoweth wrote in a recent essay. Their reasons for taking to the streets have varied widely, from protesting against corruption and an unequal playing field to calling for more investment in education, affordable housing and action on the climate crisis. Many of the first protests to make waves were in Asia and Africa.
/world/2026/nov/19/mike-lynch-superyacht.trail: From Serbia to Bangladesh and India to France, young people are pushing back against authoritarianism and reshaping political landscapes

/global-development/2026/nov/19/women-gi.headline: AI vaginas, customisable personalities and fake bruises: the sex doll market is booming. Does it matter how the dolls are treated?
/global-development/2026/nov/19/women-gi.excerpt: Two weeks ago, two distressed citizens stumbled across what they assumed was the mangled corpse of a woman, stuffed into a suitcase in a small town about three hours south of Sydney. They called the local police, who in turn issued a statement that a body in a suitcase had been found. The wider public waited sombrely for Australia’s tally of dead women to tick up by one. But instead, a day later, after forensic analysis, it was determined that the woman in question wasn’t a woman at all. The “body” was that of a sex doll, marked with fake bruises, left to rot on a lonely dirt road. In Australia, as in the UK and some other European countries, it is not illegal to own a sex doll unless it resembles a child. Given the doll’s seemingly mature presentation, police investigations were called off. The sex doll trade is flourishing. A 2026 market analysis estimates that the global market was valued at US$6.6bn in 2025, with a projection that it will more than double, to US$13.4bn, by 2033. As the market booms, and involves increasingly lifelike facsimiles of women, does how these dolls get treated matter? And when a sex doll with “bruises” and rain-matted hair is tucked into a suitcase and left on a roadside, should we be concerned?
/global-development/2026/nov/19/women-gi.trail: As the sex doll industry grows and AI changes the products available, what does it mean to engage in any kind of relationship with a woman-shaped thing?

/technology/2026/nov/18/anthropic-share-.headline: Anthropic targets valuation of up to $1.4tn in stock market flotation
/technology/2026/nov/18/anthropic-share-.excerpt: Anthropic is seeking a valuation of up to $1.4tn (£1.1tn) in its imminent stock market flotation, short of the $2tn that had been expected before investors started to question the durability of the AI boom. The developer of the Claude chatbot was widely reported to be targeting a $2tn initial public offering on Wall Street but its sights have been set lower, according to a US regulatory filing on Tuesday. Anthropic is aiming to raise up to $64.4bn by selling 825m shares in the IPO priced up to $78 a share. The California-based company will also raise a further $26bn via a separate private placement deal ⁠with cornerstone investors including the Google parent, Alphabet, and the chipmaker Nvidia. An extra $9.7bn could be raised from a so-called greenshoe offering, which kicks in if investor demand is high and would take the total amount raised by Anthropic to approximately $100bn if the shares sold at the top end of the price range. At the upper bracket of the $70-$78 per share price range, Anthropic would be worth $1.4tn on a fully diluted basis – which means taking into account all the common shares in the company in existence, including employee stock options. Trading in Anthropic shares is expected to begin next week. Investor jitters over the AI boom were crystallised last week when the US midterm elections produced victories for datacentre opponents.

/technology/2026/nov/18/anthropic-share-.headline: AI firm Anthropic to commit 5% of shares to fund for ‘public good’
/technology/2026/nov/18/anthropic-share-.excerpt: Anthropic has said it will commit 5% of its shares to a fund for the “public good”, as the AI developer behind the Claude chatbot seeks to bolster its appeal before its stock market listing. The company announced it would commit the shares, worth around $48bn (£36bn) at its latest valuation in May, subject to shareholder approval. It will add a further 2% of its stock to the fund for every 50% increase in its value above an undisclosed baseline. The fund will allow Anthropic to “explore large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations”, the company said. The move comes amid growing public nervousness about AI, from the threat to human labour to the impact on the environment and its influence on social behaviours. “AI may generate enormous economic value, but it could also cause instability for many workers,” Anthropic wrote in a blogpost. It said that while it had already committed $200m to addressing the issue, “given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed. The fund will have the versatility to pursue them.” The company, which is preparing to list on the stock market, has called for a slowdown in breakneck development of AI, a warning later echoed by rivals such as OpenAI. Anthropic was valued at $965bn in May when it raised $65bn in a funding round. The company is reportedly considering a $1.5tn valuation when it floats on the stock market, with an IPO planned for November.
/technology/2026/nov/18/anthropic-share-.trail: The $48bn giveaway comes amid concerns about the tech and as the company prepares for a stock market listing

/technology/2026/nov/18/anthropic-share-.headline: AI-linked stocks slide after tech bosses call for slowdown in ‘reckless’ development
/technology/2026/nov/18/anthropic-share-.excerpt: AI-linked stocks tumbled on Monday after the bosses of Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX called for a slowdown in AI “reckless” development, citing fears the technology could soon run out of control. Shares in the semiconductor designer Nvidia – the world’s most valuable company – were down 3.3% by market closing in New York City, while Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) slid 4% and Micron Technology and Sandisk shares slumped by 5%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq index fund was down 0.5% by the end of the day. The sell-off came after the chief executive of Anthropic, Dario Amodei, appealed at the weekend for the AI industry to “slow down”. However, Donald Trump dismissed calls to increase controls on AI as a “sick conspiracy”. In a social media post on Monday, the president wrote: “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the USA has that, in spades!” The president added that his administration had “stopped AI ‘people’ from doing bad, or potentially bad, ‘things,’ like Dario (Anthropic!)”. “There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China. WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS!”, he wrote. Trump offered a similar assessment when he called Nvidia chief, Jensen Huang, while the executive was on stage at an AI conference in California on Monday. “It’s a hoax,” Trump said via speaker phone to the audience. “The robots are not going to be taking over the world.
